A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLVR-World. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, and prompt examples, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original text-game and web-state prediction experiments, RT-1 video prediction, model analyses, web-agent control, and simulated policy evaluation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds 7B language-model results, additional video benchmarks, joint-training and transfer analyses, and PushT control results.

M1.justification: The core tokenization-and-GRPO framework remains unchanged. v2 adds a repetition-penalty reward variant, incorporates proprioceptive MSE into PushT rewards, and uses DINOv2 embeddings for comparing predicted and goal frames in PushT planning. These are localized procedural adaptations.

E1.justification: v2 adds PushT tabletop pushing and simulated Rope and Granular deformable-object prediction, substantially broadening video coverage beyond RT-1. It also evaluates goal-directed control on PushT. Existing text-game, web, and RT-1 coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's base-model and repetition-rejection video comparisons, v2 Table 4 adds R3M, ResNet, DINO CLS, DINO-WM, and AVDC comparisons. Table 12 adds control comparisons with IRIS, DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and DINO-WM. Table 4 distinguishes published baseline scores from the authors' evaluation of a public DINO-WM checkpoint.

E3.justification: New protocols include 7B text-game evaluation, dataset-specific video splits and observation histories, six-layer models for Rope/Granular, GRPO groups of 32, joint training, and PushT planning. Additionally, v1 Table 7 to v2 Table 8 changes the reported RT-1 RLVR learning rate from 1e-5 to 5e-5; unchanged existing scores do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a repetition-penalty experiment testing non-differentiable rewards and elimination of repetition. Appendix A.4.2 adds learning-curve and overfitting analyses, joint versus separate pretraining comparisons, and cross-task transfer tests after tuning on only Rope or Granular. The original metric, group-size, and test-time-scaling analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions' Table 3 reports means and standard deviations over three sampling runs; the added repetition-penalty row follows that convention. v2 introduces no new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Existing result entries are retained, while v2 adds substantial results: 7B overall accuracy of 65.53% versus 51.76% after SFT, three-dataset LPIPS/SSIM comparisons, joint-training and transfer outcomes, and PushT control success of 0.86 versus the base model's 0.80. The added penalty variant achieves zero repetition, with scaled LPIPS 13.7 versus 13.4 without the penalty.

T1.justification: The existing MDP, sequence-modeling, GRPO, MLE, and reward formalism is unchanged in substance. Writing prediction horizons using T and moving the advantage formula inline do not add mathematical reasoning. Neither version contains a theoretical development that is substantively revised in v2.

C1.justification: The abstract's scientific claims and central contribution remain stable. The introduction adds a claim of state-of-the-art performance against advanced world models, extending v1's emphasis on improvements over its pretrained base models without redefining the framework's main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops new interpretations linking Rope underperformance and eventual transfer degradation to overfitting and insufficient diverse pretraining. Section 7 adds explicit qualifications about same-dataset video pretraining and diffusion-model RL being outside the study's scope. These substantially expand the discussion of generalization mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4.2 supplies implementation information for the new benchmarks, including splits, resolutions, histories, proprioception quantization, model depth, group size, and planning embeddings. v2 also explicitly states that code, datasets, models, and video samples are available at the previously linked project website. Existing computational-resource descriptions and prompt examples are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and contextual discussion for DINO-WM, AVDC, visual encoders, the added datasets, and concurrent DanceGRPO/Flow-GRPO work. These extend comparative positioning and acknowledge related diffusion-model developments, while the existing related-work survey and central research positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction receives localized explanatory expansion, Section 7 is reorganized into algorithmic and foundation-model issues, Appendix A.4 gains dataset-specific subsections, and acknowledgements are added. Most existing prose, section order, and prompt content are preserved.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned with training-stage annotations and moved to the first page. v2 expands Tables 1 and 3, adds the benchmark comparison in Table 4, analysis Tables 9–11, control Table 12, and qualitative Figure 10. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond renumbering and pagination.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence about video-model competitiveness beyond its own RT-1 baselines. External comparisons across additional environments, joint-training and transfer tests, and PushT control evaluation strengthen the assessment of generality and practical utility. Explicit discussion of overfitting and scope limits improves calibration. Imported comparator scores and limited uncertainty reporting constrain the new claims, but do not outweigh this substantial improvement in empirical support.
